text_blocks.snippet: Residents in Central Illinois face several prominent scams, including state agency phishing texts, fake real estate listings, and high-dollar social media fraud.

list.snippet: State Agency & DMV Phishing Texts: Scammers send fraudulent text messages impersonating the Illinois Secretary of State or state treasurers. These messages falsely claim you owe money for traffic violations, tolls, or driver's license/vehicle registration suspensions, or that you have an unclaimed refund . Note: The Illinois Secretary of State never sends text messages about tolls, license suspensions, or registration fees.

Rental & Real Estate Scams: Fraudsters steal photos and addresses from legitimate online real estate sites to post fake apartment or house rentals with "too good to be true" low pricing (such as in Galesburg and surrounding areas). They often claim the owner is "out of town" and request upfront money via wire transfer, gift cards, or untraceable payment methods .
Social Media Scams: Law enforcement in areas like Peoria County report an increase in high-dollar scams originating through social media platforms.

Employment & Debt Collection Scams: Fake job listings ask for upfront personal data, training fees, or equipment purchases. Meanwhile, imposters posing as debt collectors or law enforcement use aggressive threats of arrest or wage garnishment to demand immediate payment via prepaid cards, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency.

text_blocks.snippet: How to Protect Yourself & Report Fraud

list.snippet: Do Not Click Links: Ignore and delete unexpected text messages or emails claiming you owe state fees or traffic penalties.

Verify Independently: If you suspect a message or call might be real, look up the official phone number of the agency or business independently rather than calling the number provided in the text or email.
Report phishing and online scams to the Federal Trade Commission .
Contact your local police department if you have suffered financial loss or identity theft.
Check resources or attend local safety sessions like the Peoria Heights Public Library scam prevention workshops.
